title: How to work on linen for cross-stitch
subtitle: Stitching over two threads on 28 and 32-count linen
excerpt: Linen cross-stitch is worked over two threads of the weave rather than over individual Aida squares. The resulting stitch is finer and more flexible than Aida, and the natural linen ground gives finished pieces a softer, more antique look.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, linen fabric chapter. The over-two convention is documented throughout Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A natural-fibre evenweave fabric for cross-stitch. Typically 28-count or 32-count, worked over two threads to give the same stitch size as a 14-count or 16-count Aida respectively.
The technique of working each cross-stitch over two threads of the linen or evenweave weave rather than over the holes of a structured grid fabric such as Aida.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
A blunt-tipped needle that slips between fabric threads instead of piercing them. Size 24 is the default for 14ct Aida; finer fabrics need a higher-number, finer needle.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: Linen
cross-stitch is worked
over two
threads of the weave, so each cross covers a pair of horizontal threads and a pair of vertical threads rather than a single Aida square. A 28-count
linen
worked over two gives stitches at the same scale as 14-count
Aida
; 32-count linen gives stitches at the scale of 16-count Aida.

The key difference between Aida and linen is that Aida has a clear grid of holes to aim for, while linen has a continuous weave. The over-two convention keeps each stitch consistent by using the intersection of thread pairs as the corner points of each cross. The fabric is softer, drapes better than Aida, and gives finished pieces a more natural texture. Most stitchers find 14-count Aida easier to learn on, then move to linen once the basic stitch is reliable.
Counting on linen

Hold the linen up to good light before starting. Pick out a clear vertical thread and a clear horizontal thread and trace them with your eye to confirm the weave is square (no threads are pulled out of alignment).
Find the starting point on the chart. Count the threads across from a marked fabric edge rather than counting holes, since linen has no holes.

Come up at the intersection that will be the bottom-left of the first stitch. The needle passes between threads, not through individual holes. On 28-count, the needle goes between thread 1 and thread 2 in one direction, and between thread 1 and thread 2 in the other direction.
Work the first diagonal over two threads: from the bottom-left intersection to the top-right intersection (two threads up and two threads to the right).
Complete the cross with the second diagonal going from bottom-right to top-left. Pull to the same tension as on Aida; linen is more forgiving and slightly stretchy, so avoid pulling the cross tight.
Needle and thread choices for linen
The right needle for linen is slightly larger than for the same effective stitch count on Aida. On 28-count linen, a size 24
tapestry needle
is the standard. The blunt tip parts the linen threads rather than piercing them. Use two strands of
floss
for the crosses and one strand for any back-stitch outlines.

items.symptom: Stitches look uneven, some larger than others
items.cause: Counting threads rather than thread intersections, or inadvertently stitching over one thread and then three threads.
items.fix: Slow down and count two threads forward each time. Mark the start and end threads of the first row with removable highlighter tape until the rhythm is established.

items.symptom: The fabric stretches and the stitches slide out of alignment
items.cause: The linen was not mounted firmly in the hoop before stitching.
items.fix: Mount the linen with a slightly higher tension than you would Aida. Linen stretches; Aida does not. Re-mount if the weave shifts during a long session.

content.text: What to try next

Once comfortable on 28-count linen, the next step is 32-count, which gives a finer stitch and suits pieces intended to be framed under glass. Many heirloom sampler charts were designed for linen specifically.
